# Workspace tenancy server composition

## Use when

Use this pattern when records, routes, or navigation belong to a selected
workspace and membership or role affects access.

## Do not use when

Do not use workspace tenancy for a genuinely single-owner product or as a
substitute for a simpler domain ownership column.

## Product decisions

Choose workspace creation policy, roles, invitation policy, expiry, email copy,
member permissions, personal-workspace behavior, and surface access rules.

In `workspaces` mode, `tenancyPolicy.workspace.autoProvision: true` gives every
user a personal workspace in addition to shared ones; the optional
`workspaces.personal-workspace-name` capability, a function of the user, names it. `workspaceSettings.defaults` sets
`invitesEnabled` and the colours (`lightPrimaryColor`, `darkPrimaryColor` and
the other palette fields) that new workspaces start with.

## Framework APIs

Use workspace routes, resources, scope helpers, tenancy profiles, and settings
contracts exported by `@jskit-ai/workspaces-core`.

## Role permissions

A role's `permissions` grant names that something requires:

| Grant | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `crud.<namespace>.list`, `.view`, `.create`, `.update`, `.delete` | A workspace CRUD operation; an HTTP `PATCH` is `update` |
| `crud.<namespace>.<action name>` | A custom CRUD action |
| `<prefix>.*`, `*` | Every required permission under the prefix; every permission |

At startup a grant that covers no permission an action, a route's `permission`
or a surface access policy requires stops the server outside production, with
a "did you mean"; production logs it. The check cannot see a permission the
application checks itself (a service, a row policy, `access.can()`): before
removing or renaming a reported grant, search the code for it, including built
names such as `crud.${resource}.list`. List one the application checks in
`roleCatalog.customPermissions`; remove a grant only when nothing uses it.

## Role display labels

Each `roleCatalog.roles[roleId]` definition may include an optional string
`label`. JSKIT trims it and preserves nonempty labels in role descriptors,
catalogue clones and Members/Workspace Settings responses. Labels are display
metadata; they do not inherit from a parent role. Missing, blank or non-string
labels keep the existing role-title fallback.

Shared Members invitation and member-role selectors show the label but submit
the role id. Pending invitation captions, workspace role captions and the
default invitation email use the same configured labels. Pending invitation
responses expose optional `roleLabel` alongside the unchanged `roleSid`.
Applications with their own invitation renderer may use its optional
`roleLabel` input; `roleSid` remains the stored role id.

Invitation emails use the recipient's language: `locale` is the saved
`user_settings.locale` of an existing account with the invited email, else `en`.
Renderers receive `locale` and `t(key, params)`, which renders a
`jskit.workspaces.inviteEmail.*` message from the app's
`src/locales/<code>/jskit.json` (exact locale, then language, then English); the
mailer's `sendWorkspaceInvite` receives `locale` too.

Keep existing permissions, inheritance, assignability and
`workspace.defaultInviteRole` when adding a label. `owner` remains
nonassignable. Custom roles, including specialised Training roles, are ordinary
catalogue entries. Updating labels requires no database migration.

## Transactional invitation participation

Provide one function as the optional `workspaces.invite-acceptance-participant`
capability, from a small application feature that requires only what its writes
need (it cannot require `workspaces.core`, which receives it). The built-in
`workspace.invite.redeem` action invokes `fn({ invite, user }, txOptions)`
after validating the recipient, state and expiry and activating membership in the
uncommitted transaction. Pass `txOptions` to every application owner's calls and
propagate failures. JSKIT marks accepted and commits after the function succeeds. Keep
external effects out of it. Without the capability, acceptance activates the
membership only. Allow ordinary invitations; reject stale, revoked, conflicting
or unexpectedly missing application associations.

Provide the optional `workspaces.workspace-created-participant` capability the
same way to write application records for every new workspace. The
`workspace.workspaces.create` action and personal workspace provisioning invoke
`fn({ workspace, owner }, txOptions)` after writing the workspace, its owner's
membership and its settings, in the creation's uncommitted transaction (the
caller's when it passes one). Pass `txOptions` on and propagate failures: a
failure rolls the whole creation back. An existing personal workspace does not
call it.

Call `members.prepareInvite(workspace, actor, payload, txOptions)` inside
`repositories.workspaceInvites.withTransaction(options, async (txOptions) => …)`
or another resource handle's `withTransaction`. It returns
`{ createdInviteId, inviteTokenPreview }` without delivery. Lock the workspace
with `lock(workspace.id, txOptions)` of the `workspaces` capability before
application draft/receipt rows, and save the exact invitation
association and retry receipt before commit. Failure restores the previous
pending invitation. Keep access drafts separate: preparation creates a real token.

After confirmed commit, call `members.sendInvite(workspace, actor, prepared,
{ context })`. A later attempt can pass only `{ createdInviteId }`. Delivery
reloads the committed pending invitation and uses its saved recipient, role and
expiry. `inviteDelivery` reports `mailer_unconfigured`, `failed` on a renderer/mailer
exception, or the normalized mailer result. Persistence is unchanged by delivery
failure. A provider may accept a message before failing; the application owns
receipts and retries. Keep tokens/URLs out of logs and use controlled mailers in tests.

`createInvite`, acceptance and refusal own their managed transactions and
refuse a call made inside one (`withTransaction({ ...options, outermost: true }, work)`). Use preparation followed by delivery after commit for
transactional creation; put related acceptance writes in the participant. Revocation may join
a managed transaction. Raw Knex/savepoint transactions cannot own resource
writes. Invitation mutations lock workspace then invitation rows, revalidate
current state and reject changes to accepted/revoked invitations. Expiry rejection
for the matching recipient commits revocation before returning 409. Preserve transaction
outcomes and causes; a completion-hook error after commit cannot undo writes.

See the human guide's **Workspace tenancy → Transactional invitation
participation** for the full consumer example, errors, controlled mailer,
compatibility notes and native verification commands. Application services own
authorization, identity/training linking, scope eligibility and required audit.

## Invariants

- Workspace membership and role are checked before scoped application actions.
- Role ids are stable product vocabulary shared by server and client config.
- Invitation tokens remain secret; emails receive only the intended link.
- Workspace scope reaches repository queries, not just route parsing.
- Package-owned migrations run directly from the installed package graph.

## Example files

`example/config/roles.js` is a concrete role catalogue, set as the
application's `roleCatalog` config.

The invitation email comes from two optional `workspaces.core` capabilities,
which one small application feature provides:
`example/packages/main/src/server/WorkspaceInvitationsFeature.js`.

```js
provides: {
  inviteEmailTemplate: "workspaces.invite-email-template",
  inviteMailer: "workspaces.invite-mailer"
},
setup({ env }) {
  return {
    inviteEmailTemplate: renderWorkspaceInviteEmail,
    inviteMailer: createWorkspaceInviteMailer({ env })
  };
}
```

- `email/workspaceInviteEmail.js` is the renderer, a
  `WorkspaceInviteEmailTemplate` returning `{ subject, text, html }`.
- `email/workspaceInviteMailer.js` is the mailer, a `WorkspaceInviteMailer`
  whose `sendWorkspaceInvite` sends the rendered message over SMTP.

Without a renderer, workspaces-core uses its built-in email; without a mailer,
invitations are created and their delivery reports `mailer_unconfigured`. The
feature must not require `workspaces.core`, which receives both.

## Variation points

Change roles, invitation policy and copy, defaults, access policies, surface
ids, and product-specific workspace settings.

## Verification

Test create/list/select, member and non-member access, each role boundary,
invitation expiry/redemption, cross-workspace isolation, and email output.

## Avoid

- synthetic membership workarounds
- authorizing from client navigation state
- embedding invitation templates or secrets in package metadata
- source-appending install commands
